question: When brakes stop a moving vehicle, its energy is changed mainly into what?
explanation: Brakes turn the energy of a moving vehicle into heat, which the drums, rotors and other brake parts must absorb and get rid of. Too much heat leads to fade and failure.

question: One brake on a truck is not working. What does this do to the other brakes?
optionA: They lose some of their air pressure
explanation: The Official Air Brake Handbook warns that a single malfunctioning brake increases the work of all the others, so they overheat quickly and may fail too.

question: Before you take brake measurements after a long run, the brake assembly should be:
explanation: The handbook notes that brake assemblies should be cool to the touch before you attempt any brake measurements. Drums also expand as they heat up.

question: Why are air brakes used on large commercial vehicles?
optionB: They work with no delay at all
optionD: They carry high force a long way
explanation: Air brakes can develop and transmit high mechanical forces over great distances with simple parts and connections. They do have a split-second delay and must be inspected.

question: Why does a hydraulic brake act at the wheels the moment you press the pedal?
optionB: Brake fluid is kept under heat
optionC: The brake lines are very short
explanation: Brake fluid cannot be compressed, so force reaches each wheel directly. Air must travel through the system, which causes a short delay in air brakes.

question: In which air brake systems is there a split-second delay in brake reaction?
explanation: The handbook says this delay in brake reaction occurs in all air brake systems, because compressed air must move from one part of the system to another.

question: On a disc air brake, what do the brake pads press against?
optionA: The inner face of a drum
explanation: Disc brakes use a rotor and a caliper holding the pads. The pads press toward each other, clamping both sides of the rotor. Drum brakes press shoes against a drum.

question: Air-over-hydraulic brakes are used mainly on what kind of vehicle?
explanation: Air-over-hydraulic brakes, compressed air working with a hydraulic system, are used mainly on medium-duty commercial vehicles.

question: Do you need a Z endorsement in Ontario to drive a vehicle with air-over-hydraulic brakes?
optionB: No, only for full air brakes
explanation: In Ontario you must have an air brake endorsement on your licence to drive a vehicle with air-over-hydraulic brakes, as well as one with full air brakes.

question: A school bus has hydraulic service brakes and an air-operated parking brake only. Does its driver need a Z endorsement for the brakes?
explanation: The handbook says you do not need an air brake endorsement to drive a vehicle with air parking brakes, where all other braking is hydraulic.

question: Which of these is not one of the three types of foundation brake in the handbook?
explanation: The handbook lists three types of foundation brake: S cam, disc and wedge. Band brakes are not one of them.

question: On an S cam brake, the slack adjuster is attached to the end of what?
explanation: Pushrod stroke acts on the slack adjuster fixed to the end of the camshaft, which turns the camshaft so the S shaped head spreads the shoes.

question: What is the job of the brake spider in an S cam brake?
explanation: The brake spider is the main mounting base for the brake shoes. Return springs pull the shoes back, and the slack adjuster turns the camshaft.

question: What do the camshaft rollers in an S cam brake do?
optionA: Hold the drum on the hub
optionB: Move the shoes in and out
explanation: The rollers rotate with the camshaft while moving the brake shoes outward and inward. The return spring keeps the rollers against the camshaft head.

question: In an S cam brake, what pulls the shoes back to the released position?
explanation: A return spring pulls the brake shoes in to the released position and keeps the camshaft rollers in contact with the camshaft head.

question: Which part of an S cam brake sits outside the wheel, where a driver can easily see it?
explanation: External parts include the brake chamber, slack adjuster, pushrod and camshaft shaft. Rollers, anchor springs and the spider sit inside the wheel.

question: Which type of foundation brake has no exposed brake linkage?
explanation: Wedge brakes are drum brakes whose chamber pushrods face inward and slide a wedge between the shoes, so no linkage is exposed. S cam brakes have an exposed pushrod.

question: Wedge air brakes are designed to be:
explanation: The handbook says wedge air brakes are designed to be self-adjusting.

question: Which part do disc air brakes use that S cam brakes do not?
explanation: All disc air brakes use calipers and rotors. Both designs can use brake chambers, pushrods and slack adjusters.

question: Can one vehicle use more than one design of foundation brake?
optionA: No, only one design per vehicle
optionD: Yes, even on the same vehicle
explanation: The handbook says an air brake system can work with several designs of foundation brake, even on the same vehicle.

question: What powers the air compressor in an air brake system?
explanation: The compressor is powered by the engine, either directly or through belts and pulleys, and is mounted on the engine or on brackets and fasteners.

question: How does an air compressor raise the pressure of the air?
optionA: It heats the air inside the tank
optionB: It forces air into a smaller space
optionC: It adds alcohol vapour to it
optionD: It cools the air in a dryer first
explanation: The compressor draws in air at normal pressure and forces it into a much smaller space, so its pressure rises. The compressed air is stored energy.

question: Which part sets the points at which the compressor starts and stops pumping air?
explanation: The governor makes the compressor stop pumping at cut-out pressure and start again at cut-in pressure. The safety valve only vents if the governor fails.

question: Cut-out pressure is normally how far above cut-in pressure?
explanation: The handbook says cut-out is normally 138 to 173 kPa (20 to 25 psi) above cut-in, and the two points set the normal pressure range.

question: A normal air brake system pressure range is around:
explanation: The handbook gives a normal range of around 690 to 828 kPa (100 to 120 psi). Drivers should know the range of their own vehicle and report anything abnormal.

question: Actual cut-out pressure must never be higher than:
explanation: Actual cut-out pressure must never exceed 1000 kPa (145 psi). 1035 kPa (150 psi) is where safety valves normally open, which is not a cut-out setting.

question: Actual cut-in pressure must never be less than:
explanation: Actual cut-in pressure must never be below 552 kPa (80 psi). 380 kPa (55 psi) is the limit for the low air-pressure warning, a different figure.

question: You stopped because air pressure fell below the normal cut-in point. When may you drive on?
optionB: Once the wet tank is drained
optionC: When the warning light goes out
optionD: When pressure and brakes are normal
explanation: The handbook says to proceed only when air pressure returns to its normal operating range and all other air brake functions are normal.

question: Which tank does air from the compressor enter first?
explanation: The first tank is the supply tank. From there the air splits into the primary and secondary (dual-service) tanks.

question: Why is the supply tank also called the wet tank?
optionA: It is the one drained by hand
optionB: It collects most moisture and oil
optionC: It holds the alcohol for winter
optionD: It sits closest to the wheels
explanation: Moisture and compressor oil drop out of the air as it is compressed, and most of it settles in the first tank, the supply or wet tank.

question: How can too much moisture and oil in the air tanks lead to brake failure?
optionC: It reduces the volume of air
explanation: The handbook lists this among the problems: too much moisture and oil in the tanks reduces the volume of air and may cause brake failure.

question: Where is the drain valve on an air tank?
optionA: On the top of the tank
optionD: At the bottom of the tank
explanation: Each tank has its drain valve at the bottom, where the moisture and oil settle.

question: Why should the supply tank be drained before the other tanks?
optionA: So its moisture does not pass on
optionB: So the governor cuts in sooner
optionC: So the dryer can purge itself
explanation: Draining the supply tank first removes the moisture it has collected before it can flow into the next tank or farther into the system.

question: What does a one-way check valve do in the air supply subsystem?
explanation: Air leaving the supply tank is kept from returning by one-way check valves, so a leak on one side cannot empty the other.

question: Why do air brake systems split the air into primary and secondary circuits?
optionA: One circuit serves the trailer only
optionB: One circuit feeds the spring brakes only
optionC: Either can stop it if one fails
optionD: One circuit stores air for the horn
explanation: Two delivery circuits are a safety feature: if one fails, the other gives enough braking to stop the vehicle.

question: The primary and secondary tanks are also called:
explanation: They are called dry tanks because they collect less moisture than the supply or wet tank.

question: Where is an air dryer fitted in the system?
explanation: The air dryer sits between the compressor and the supply tank, so moisture is removed before the air enters the supply tank.

question: When does an air dryer expel the moisture it has collected?
optionA: When the engine is shut off
optionC: When the cut-in point is reached
optionD: Each time the pedal is pressed
explanation: Moisture collected in the dryer is blown out with high-pressure air when the compressor reaches cut-out pressure.

question: A truck has an air dryer. Do its air tanks still need draining?
explanation: The handbook says vehicles with air dryers must still have their air tanks drained regularly.

question: What does an alcohol evaporator do in an air brake system?
optionA: Removes oil from the supply tank
explanation: It adds alcohol vapour that mixes with moisture or ice in the system and reduces its tendency to freeze, which could cause brake failure.

question: What may be put into an alcohol evaporator?
explanation: The handbook says only products specifically designed for this use may be put into an alcohol evaporator.

question: A safety valve on the supply tank is venting air. What does this mean?
explanation: A venting safety valve means too much pressure is building, usually because the governor failed to cut out, and it needs immediate repair.

question: The low air-pressure warning must come on before pressure in either tank falls to:
explanation: In Ontario the warning must activate before pressure falls to 380 kPa (55 psi), though most devices come on at 414 kPa (60 psi) or higher.

question: What kind of signal must a low air-pressure warning device give?
optionA: A sound only, such as a buzzer
optionB: A pulse through the brake pedal
optionD: A visual one, such as a light
explanation: The warning must be visual, such as a light, and may also use a buzzer, bell or alarm.

question: On a vehicle with a wig wag, what happens when air pressure is too low?
explanation: A wig wag is a low-pressure warning device whose arm drops into the driver's view when air pressure is too low.

question: Why should you stay out of the path of air exhausting from brake valves?
optionA: It is hot enough to burn skin
optionB: It carries debris at high speed
optionD: It is toxic to breathe in
explanation: Exhausting air travels very fast and carries moisture, oil, dirt and dust that can harm your eyes and hearing, and it sprays debris up from the ground.

question: Which of these is not a place where an air brake system exhausts compressed air?
explanation: The handbook lists brake valve exhaust ports, points on or near the axles, the air-dryer exhaust port and tank drain valves while draining.

question: Why does an air brake system need a governor?
optionA: The tanks would fill up with oil
optionB: The brakes would release too slowly
optionD: The compressor would make too much air
explanation: Compressors run whenever the engine runs and could make far more air than needed. The governor stops pumping at cut-out and reduces the load on the engine.

question: Vehicles with air brakes must have separate brake systems for which two jobs?
optionB: Front axle, and rear axle stopping
explanation: Air brake vehicles must have separate, independently controlled systems for normal stopping (service brakes) and for parking and emergency braking.

question: What happens when you press the brake pedal harder?
optionA: Air flows to the brakes for longer
optionB: More air pressure reaches the brakes
optionD: The spring brakes start to release
explanation: The pedal valve opens farther as you press harder, delivering higher air pressure to the service brakes and more braking force at the wheels.

question: On a dual-circuit system, which wheels get their air from the primary circuit?
explanation: The handbook says the wheels supplied by the primary or secondary circuit vary by vehicle manufacturer.

question: What does the handbook say about colour codes on air brake hoses and tubes?
optionA: Every brake hose must be red
optionC: One colour is used for all hoses
optionD: Older vehicles may not follow them
explanation: Hoses and tubes come in many colours, sizes and styles. Manufacturers now follow an industry colour code, but older vehicles may not.

question: A service brake chamber holds a pushrod, a return spring and a flexible rubber disc called a:
explanation: Air fills the chamber and moves the diaphragm, which pushes out the pushrod to apply the brake.

question: When air pressure is released from a service brake chamber, what returns the pushrod?
explanation: A return spring inside the service brake chamber pushes the pushrod back to its original position when the air is released.

question: The lever that links the pushrod to the brake assembly is called the:
explanation: The pushrod and the lever called the slack adjuster link the brake chamber to the brake assembly and pass the pushrod motion on to the shoes or pads.

question: What does stroke length measure?
optionA: How far the brake pedal moves
optionB: The length of the slack adjuster
optionC: The width of the brake chamber
optionD: How far the pushrod travels out
explanation: Pushrod stroke is the pushrod extending from the chamber, and stroke length is the distance it travels out.

question: As brake application pressure rises from 69 kPa (10 psi) to 552 kPa (80 psi), the pushrod stroke:
explanation: Stroke depends on the air pressure entering the chamber; the handbook's example is that it increases noticeably from 69 to 552 kPa.

question: What happens if a pushrod has to travel beyond its chamber's stroke capacity?
optionB: No more brake force is made
optionC: The wheel locks up at once
explanation: Each chamber has a limited stroke capacity, beyond which no brake force is produced. That is why linkage must be kept adjusted.

question: As brakes wear, the brake linkage must be re-adjusted so that:
optionA: The drums stay below a set heat
optionB: The pedal stays at one height
optionC: Stroke stays in its normal range
optionD: Air loss stays under the limit
explanation: Brake wear lengthens the stroke, so the linkage is re-adjusted at regular intervals to keep the pushrod stroke within its normal operating range.

question: What does a front wheel-limiting valve do?
explanation: Front wheel-limiting valves reduce the force of the service brakes on the front steering axle.

question: Almost all commercial vehicles use which kind of brake chamber?
explanation: Almost all commercial vehicles use chambers held together by a clamp assembly, called clamp-type brake chambers. The handbook's adjustment chart covers these.

question: Where are the air brake chambers on a vehicle?
explanation: Air brake chambers are round metal containers at each wheel, where compressed air becomes the force that applies the brakes.

question: A brake's pushrod stroke is past its adjustment limit. How does the handbook class this?
explanation: The handbook says any brake exceeding the adjustment limit is a defect that requires prompt attention, because brake force can drop sharply.

question: Why must you identify a brake chamber's type and size?
optionA: To order the right air hose
explanation: Chambers come in many styles, types and sizes, and each has its own adjustment limit, so you must identify both to know the right limit.

question: How are the spring brakes in a spring brake chamber released?
optionB: A hand lever turns the camshaft
explanation: Spring brakes apply when air leaves the chamber and release when enough air pressure builds to compress, or cage, the large coil spring.

question: About how much air pressure is normally needed to keep the spring brakes released?
explanation: Normally about 414 kPa (60 psi) is needed to cage the spring. Below that, the spring brakes start to apply.

question: In a spring brake chamber, which section is nearest the pushrod end?
explanation: The spring section is piggy-backed onto the service section. The part nearest the pushrod is the service brake section, which works like a separate service chamber.

question: How can you tell a spring brake chamber from a service brake chamber by sight?
optionA: It has a red clamp ring
explanation: To fit the large coil spring, a clearly visible section is added to the service chamber, which makes it significantly bigger.

question: Why can some vehicles still move with their spring brakes applied?
optionB: They only work on the trailer
optionD: They act on the front axle only
explanation: The handbook notes that many vehicles can be driven with the spring brakes on, because spring brakes do not have the braking power of a full service brake application.

question: Why should a driver never try to service a spring brake chamber?
optionA: It is full of hot brake fluid
explanation: The coil spring is compressed under very high tension. Tampering, damage or corrosion can release it with sudden, violent motion of chamber parts.

question: A spring brake chamber has a caging bolt sticking out of it. What does this tell you?
explanation: A technician can cage the spring with a caging bolt to disable a failed chamber. A disabled chamber looks different and its parking and emergency brake will not apply.

question: You find a disabled (caged) spring brake chamber on your truck. What should you do?
explanation: The handbook says a driver who finds a disabled spring brake chamber should have the vehicle inspected and repaired immediately.

question: Who may manually cage a spring brake to move a vehicle in an emergency?
explanation: The handbook says a technician can manually compress or cage the spring using a caging bolt or similar mechanism.

question: On most spring brake control valves, what does pulling the knob out do?
explanation: Most control valves are pushed to supply air and release the spring brakes, and pulled to exhaust air and apply them.

question: Some vehicles reverse the push and pull functions of the spring brake control. Where are they usually shown?
optionC: On or near the control valve
explanation: The handbook says the valve's functions are normally described on or near the control valve, and drivers must know the type used in their vehicle.

question: What does a separate tractor parking-brake control valve let you do?
explanation: This optional control releases the spring brakes on the tractor while the trailer spring brakes stay applied.

question: The optional tractor parking-brake control valve normally has which knob?
explanation: The handbook says the tractor parking-brake control valve normally has a round blue knob.

question: What kind of stop does an automatic spring brake application from low air pressure cause?
optionC: No stop on a level road
optionD: A stop of the trailer only
explanation: When pressure drops below the set level, the control valve exhausts the air holding the springs released, causing a sudden automatic application and an uncontrolled stop.

question: Your service brakes fail while driving. What can you use to apply the spring brakes?
explanation: In an emergency when the service brakes fail, the spring brakes can be applied with the spring brake control valve. The trailer hand valve must never be used for emergency stops.

question: What does the effectiveness of a vehicle's spring brakes depend on?
explanation: If the brakes are out of adjustment, the spring brakes may not stop or hold the vehicle. Their effectiveness depends on brake condition and proper adjustment.

question: Which vehicles commonly use DD3 safety actuators for parking and emergency brakes?
explanation: Many buses and motor coaches use the DD3 Safety Actuator, which does not use a large spring in the brake chamber.

question: How many air line connections does a DD3 brake chamber have?
explanation: A DD3 chamber has three air line connections, where a conventional spring brake chamber has two.

question: How does a DD3 chamber hold the brake applied?
optionD: With a wedge on the drum
explanation: Internally, DD3 chambers have a mechanical means of locking the brake in the applied position instead of a large spring.

question: To release DD3 parking brakes, after operating the control valve you press the brake pedal for about:
explanation: The handbook says releasing them requires operating the control valve and then pressing the brake pedal for three to five seconds.

question: In most current spring brake chambers, how easy is it to release the spring by accident?
explanation: The handbook says that, due to the way most spring brake chambers are now built, it is very difficult to release the spring unintentionally.

question: What can cause the spring in a spring brake chamber to release suddenly?
optionC: Low tire pressure on that wheel
explanation: Tampering, damage or corrosion can cause the spring to release, with sudden violent motion of chamber parts.

question: Which vehicles with air brakes must have a way of stopping if the service brakes fail?
explanation: All vehicles with air brakes must have a way of stopping if the service brake system fails.

question: Most vehicle makers combine the emergency braking system with what?
explanation: Most manufacturers combine emergency braking with the parking brake, using spring brakes for both jobs.

question: How many air line connections join a trailer's brake system to the towing vehicle?
explanation: Two connections are made: the supply (emergency) line, which fills the trailer tanks, and the service line, which carries service brake pressure.

question: Which trailer line carries air to fill the trailer's tanks?
explanation: The supply or emergency line fills the trailer's tanks. The service line carries the pressure that applies the trailer service brakes.

question: What does the trailer service line carry?
optionA: Air to fill the trailer tanks
optionB: Air for the spring brakes only
explanation: The service line carries pressure for the trailer service brakes whenever you press the pedal or use the hand valve.

question: The metal trailer couplers on the air lines are commonly called:
explanation: The two pairs of metal trailer couplers are called gladhands. Each has a flexible seal for a leak-free connection.

question: What are dead-end (dummy) couplers on a towing vehicle for?
optionB: Sealing off the trailer air tanks
optionC: Locking the trailer to the tractor
explanation: Dead-end or dummy couplers are receptacles that protect the couplers from dirt and water when no trailer is connected.

question: In most cases, the service line coupler is colour-coded:
explanation: Couplers are usually colour-coded during manufacturing: red for the supply line and blue for the service line.

question: What happens if the trailer air lines are cross-connected?
explanation: With cross-connected lines the spring brakes may not release, the towing vehicle may lose air and the service brakes will not work properly. It is not safe to drive.

question: Why do the rear supply and service lines on a lead trailer usually have shut-off valves?
optionA: To apply the rear trailer brakes
optionB: To drain water from the lines
optionC: To test the trailer spring brakes
optionD: To prevent air loss when unused
explanation: When a second trailer is not connected, manual shut-off valves keep air from escaping through these extra lines.

question: The brake system on a converter dolly is essentially the same as which system?
explanation: The handbook says a converter dolly's brake system is essentially the same as a trailer system.

question: What does the trailer hand valve apply?
explanation: The hand valve lets the driver apply the trailer service brakes independently of the towing vehicle's brakes.

question: You use the trailer hand valve and the brake pedal at the same time. What does the trailer get?
explanation: When both are used, the trailer receives the higher pressure, sent through the service line.

question: When may the trailer hand valve be used to hold a parked combination?
explanation: The handbook says trailer hand valves must never be used for parking or emergency stops.

question: How do you open the trailer supply valve to send air to a trailer?
explanation: The trailer supply valve is a push/pull valve that is pushed in to open and supply air to the trailer, and pulled out to close.

question: There is no trailer attached. How should the trailer supply valve be set?
explanation: With no trailer attached the valve should be closed (pulled out). Leaving it open lets a large amount of air escape.

question: Why might the trailer supply valve close by itself before the dash gauges fall to 311 kPa (45 psi)?
optionA: The governor closes it at cut-in
optionB: The low air warning closes it
optionC: Line pressure is below tank pressure
optionD: The tractor spring brakes close it
explanation: With air rushing out of the supply line, line pressure is much lower than tank pressure, so the valve usually closes well before the gauges reach that range.

question: What is the job of the tractor (towing vehicle) protection valve?
optionA: Keeping air in the trailer tanks
optionD: Keeping air in the towing vehicle
explanation: It ensures that an air loss in the trailer does not drain the air from the towing vehicle.

question: What controls the tractor protection valve?
explanation: Opening the trailer supply valve directs air to open the tractor protection valve. Closing it exhausts that air and the protection valve closes.

question: When the trailer supply valve is closed, the tractor protection valve closes by:
explanation: When the supply valve is closed, air exhausts from the tractor protection valve and it closes by spring force.

question: Trailer spring brakes must apply automatically when supply line pressure drops below:
explanation: The handbook says the trailer spring brakes must apply automatically when air pressure in the trailer supply line drops below 414 kPa (60 psi).

question: Which event should make the trailer spring brakes apply automatically?
explanation: Supply line pressure drops when the line ruptures or disconnects, or when the driver closes the supply valve, and the trailer spring brakes apply.

question: The trailer service brakes fail in an emergency. How can you apply the trailer spring brakes?
optionD: Push in the tractor parking knob
explanation: In an emergency the trailer spring brakes can be applied by closing the trailer supply valve. The hand valve works the service brakes, which have failed.

question: On a trailer with spring brake priority, which tank fills first?
explanation: With spring brake priority, air from the towing vehicle first fills the spring brake tank to a set pressure before filling the service brake tank.

question: What is the risk with a spring brake priority trailer?
optionA: Its spring brakes may never release
optionB: Its tanks may never fully drain
optionC: It may move without service brakes
explanation: A spring brake priority trailer can be towed before the service brake tanks fill, so it may be on the road without enough air to work its service brakes.

question: What does service brake priority make sure of before a trailer can be towed?
explanation: Service brake priority fills the service brake tank first, so enough air is available for the service brakes before the spring brakes can release.

question: Your truck is heavily loaded and moving fast. To meet the higher braking demand, you must:
explanation: More weight or speed means the brakes must do more work, which needs greater application pressure. You get it by pressing the pedal farther.

question: You double your vehicle's weight. What happens to its stopping distance?
explanation: The handbook says stopping distance increases in proportion to any increase in weight, so double the weight means double the distance.

question: You double your vehicle's speed. What happens to its stopping distance?
optionB: It becomes eight times as long
optionC: It becomes four times as long
optionD: It becomes three times as long
explanation: Stopping distance grows faster than speed. Doubling speed increases the stopping distance by four times.

question: You double both your vehicle's weight and its speed. Stopping distance becomes how many times longer?
explanation: Double weight doubles the distance and double speed quadruples it, so together the distance increases by eight times (2 x 4).

question: What can happen when a vehicle is loaded beyond its rated weight?
explanation: Overloading can exceed the brake system's capacity, so the brakes may not be able to stop the vehicle safely.

question: Why must air brake lag be counted when you choose a following distance?
optionB: Brakes act a split second late
optionD: Brakes lag only with a trailer
explanation: All air brake systems have a split-second delay in application and release, up to about one-half second, which must be allowed for in following distance.

question: Which driving situation does the handbook name as raising brake temperatures?
explanation: Repeated braking, such as on a long or steep hill or in stop-and-go traffic, and severe braking raise brake temperatures above normal.

question: Which driving habit reduces harsh braking and heat build-up in the brakes?
optionA: Braking hard at the last moment
explanation: The handbook says keeping a safe distance behind other vehicles reduces harsh brake use and excessive heat in the brakes.

question: Engine brakes, retarders and auxiliary brakes slow the vehicle using:
optionB: Extra air from the supply tank
optionD: A second set of brake shoes
explanation: These devices use engine compression or hydraulic or electric means to slow the vehicle and help keep brake temperatures down.

question: In extreme cases, what can severe brake fade lead to?
optionB: Being unable to slow or stop
explanation: Brake fade can become so severe, on a long hill at excessive speed or with an overload, that you may be unable to slow or stop the vehicle.

question: Brake fade is most likely when you are:
optionA: Driving on a flat, open highway
optionB: Starting off from a full stop
optionC: Going down a long hill too fast
explanation: Heat from heavy or repeated braking causes fade. The handbook's extreme example is travelling down a long hill at excessive speed or with an overloaded vehicle.

question: Full braking capacity is seldom needed in normal driving. What must still be true?
optionA: It may be reduced on empty runs
optionB: It is needed only with a trailer
optionC: It is checked only at renewal
explanation: Full brake capacity is not often needed, but for safety it must always be available, which is why brakes must stay correctly adjusted.

question: When a brake's pushrod stroke becomes excessive, what happens to the brake force at that wheel?
explanation: Brake force drops significantly when stroke becomes excessive, and past the adjustment limit it falls off rapidly toward zero.

question: When is a small loss of braking from poor adjustment most likely to show up?
explanation: A small loss is unlikely to be noticed in normal driving. It may only show with heavier loads, higher speeds, long downgrades or emergency stops.

question: How can you find out that your brakes are out of adjustment?
optionA: By the feel of the pedal
optionD: By listening for any brake noise
explanation: The handbook says brakes that are out of adjustment cannot be detected except by a reliable inspection method.

question: What does ABS do when it senses an abnormal drop in a wheel's speed?
optionA: Sends more air to that wheel
explanation: A sudden drop in wheel speed signals possible wheel lock, so ABS reduces brake force to that wheel to prevent a skid and keep steering control.

question: Compared with the same vehicle without ABS, what should you expect of stopping distance with ABS?
optionD: It will be shorter on ice
explanation: ABS helps prevent wheel lock but you should not expect a shorter stopping distance. On clean dry roads you will notice no difference.

question: Where are the ABS indicators on a trailer usually mounted?
explanation: On trailers, ABS indicators are usually mounted where they are visible in the driver's rear-view mirror.

question: Which of these does not increase the demand on a vehicle's brakes?
explanation: Demand on the brakes rises with weight and speed and with long downgrades. A lighter load reduces it.

question: Besides brake fade and brake failure, what can too much brake heat cause?
explanation: The handbook warns that too much heat can lead to brake fade, brake failure and even a tire fire.

question: A vehicle with air brakes does not comply with the Highway Traffic Act and regulations. What must happen?
optionA: It must not be driven on any road
optionB: It may finish the day's route
optionC: It may be driven to its next stop
optionD: It may be driven if it is empty
explanation: When a vehicle fails to comply, the driver, operator and owner must ensure it is not driven on any road or highway.

question: Penalties for operating a vehicle that does not comply with the Act can range from:
optionC: A fine to a road test
optionD: A demerit point to a fine
explanation: The handbook says penalties may range from a fine to vehicle detainment or impoundment.

question: Who can be charged when a vehicle with a defective air brake system is operated?
optionD: Only the driver at the time
explanation: Operating a vehicle with defects, or failing to do the required inspections, can result in charges against the driver and/or operator.

question: Why park on a level surface to inspect an air brake system?
optionA: The gauges read wrong on a slope
optionB: Drain valves only work when level
optionC: Air leaks are louder on a slope
optionD: Some steps need the parking brakes off
explanation: Some inspection steps are done with the parking brakes released, and a level surface reduces the chance of the vehicle moving unexpectedly.

question: When must wheel chocks or blocks be used during an inspection?
optionA: Leaving the seat, parking brakes off
explanation: The handbook says chocks or blocks must be used whenever a test or inspection requires the driver to leave the seat with the parking brakes released.

question: By law, to whom must a driver report a defect in the air brake system?
explanation: Drivers are required by law to report any air brake defects to the vehicle operator.

question: You see that a brake lining does not touch the drum when the brakes are applied. What does this show?
explanation: The lining must press against the drum when applied and be clear of it when released. Lining that does not contact the drum when applied indicates a malfunctioning brake.

question: A brake lining has grease on it from a leaking wheel seal. The lining is:
optionA: Fine once it is wiped clean
optionB: Defective only if also worn thin
optionC: A concern only in wet weather
explanation: Grease or oil on the lining causes abnormal brake behaviour. The handbook says lining contaminated with grease or oil is defective.

question: A brake chamber's size number is based on what?
explanation: The size of an air brake chamber is based on the area of its diaphragm in square inches.

question: On a steering axle, why must the brake chambers at each end be the same size?
optionD: The ABS sensors need them matched
explanation: Matching sizes keep brake forces balanced on each end of an axle, which matters most on a steering axle, where imbalance can affect the steering.

question: When should a brake chamber be checked for air leaks?
optionA: Spring brakes on, service brakes off
optionC: Spring brakes off, service brakes on
explanation: Chambers must be checked with air in them: spring brakes released and service brakes applied. Leaks can usually be heard.

question: A brake chamber has small, round vent holes made by its manufacturer. What does this mean?
explanation: Manufactured vent holes are not a concern. Holes or cracks from impact or other damage mean the chamber is defective.

question: A slack adjuster's effective length is the distance between:
explanation: Effective length is from the centre of the camshaft to the clevis pin. Using a different pushrod hole changes it.

question: Why must the slack adjusters at both ends of a steering axle have the same effective length?
optionA: To keep stroke under the limit
explanation: Slack adjusters act as levers that multiply chamber force, so unequal effective lengths on one axle give unbalanced braking.

question: A hose's outer cover is worn through to the reinforcing fabric, but no leak can be heard yet. The hose is:
optionB: Fine if it is wrapped in tape
optionD: A concern only on a trailer
explanation: When damage extends into the reinforcing or inner layer, the air line is defective. Damaged or worn lines are a concern even before a leak appears.

question: An air line was repaired with an ordinary hardware fitting not made for air brakes. This is:
optionA: Allowed if it does not leak
optionB: Prohibited only on the service line
optionC: Allowed for one trip to a shop
explanation: Air brake systems need fittings specifically designed and approved for that use. Improper fittings or improper repairs are prohibited.

question: How should you check that an air tank is securely mounted?
optionA: Look at it and try to move it
optionB: Drain it and listen for leaks
optionC: Tap it and listen for rust
optionD: Check its pressure on the gauge
explanation: Check both by looking and by attempting to move the tank, and check the brackets and hardware. Unusual movement suggests an insecure tank or bracket.

question: An air compressor should be inspected with the engine:
explanation: The handbook says air compressors must always be inspected with the engine stopped.

question: How should a good compressor drive belt respond to firm hand pressure?
optionA: It does not move at all
explanation: The belt should give slightly under firm hand pressure. Excessive movement means it is too loose. A loose, cut or frayed belt is defective.

question: Which brake drum condition must a driver look for during an inspection?
explanation: Drivers must inspect drums and rotors for damage, cracks or breaks. A cracked or broken drum or rotor is a defect.

question: Before you begin an inspection of air brake operation, how do you secure the vehicle?
optionA: Apply spring brakes and chock wheels
optionC: Drain the tanks and chock wheels
optionD: Set the hand valve and let it idle
explanation: Park on level ground, apply the spring brakes and put wheel chocks or blocks in place before you start.

question: You may leave the driver's seat or get under the vehicle only when:
optionB: Spring brakes on or wheels blocked
explanation: The handbook says never leave the seat or get under a vehicle unless its spring brakes are applied or the wheels are securely blocked.

question: To test the low air-pressure warning, air pressure should first be:
explanation: Begin the test with pressure above 621 kPa (90 psi), engine stopped or running, then lower it until the warning comes on.

question: During the low air warning test, why must the ignition be on?
explanation: If the ignition key is not turned on the warning will not activate, so the engine may run or be off but the ignition must be on.

question: In the low air warning test, the warning comes on at 400 kPa on both gauges. What is the result?
explanation: The device passes if it activates at or above 380 kPa (55 psi) on both the primary and secondary gauges. 400 kPa is above that.

question: In the low air warning test, the warning stays off until the secondary gauge reads 360 kPa. What is the result?
optionC: It passes if the primary is fine
explanation: It fails if it does not activate until below 380 kPa (55 psi) on either the primary or the secondary gauge. 360 kPa is below that.

question: To start the air-pressure build-up test, first lower the system pressure to below:
explanation: Reduce pressure below 552 kPa (80 psi), then time the rise from 587 to 690 kPa (85 to 100 psi) with the engine at 600 to 900 rpm.

question: During the build-up test, what engine speed should you hold?
explanation: Keep the engine idling between 600 and 900 rpm while you time the pressure rise.

question: In the build-up test, you time the pressure rise between which two readings?
explanation: You note the time when pressure reaches 587 kPa (85 psi) and again at 690 kPa (100 psi).

question: What is the longest the build-up from 587 to 690 kPa (85 to 100 psi) may take?
explanation: The vehicle passes if build-up time is two minutes or less, and fails if it takes longer.

question: In the build-up test, pressure rises from 587 to 690 kPa in 1 minute 50 seconds. What is the result?
optionA: Fails, it is over the limit
optionB: Fails, it must be under 60 seconds
optionC: Passes, it is within the limit
explanation: The limit is two minutes. 1 minute 50 seconds is within it, so the vehicle passes.

question: A trailer is attached when you do the build-up test. What should you do first?
explanation: With a trailer attached, ensure the trailer supply valve is closed (pulled out) before timing the build-up.

question: During the governor test, how can you tell the compressor has reached cut-out?
explanation: Air pressure gauges stop climbing at compressor cut-out.

question: On a vehicle with an air dryer, what else tells you the compressor has reached cut-out?
explanation: When a vehicle uses an air dryer, its exhaust (purge) cycle also indicates that the compressor has reached the cut-out setting.

question: In the governor test, pressure stops climbing at 1030 kPa (149 psi). What is the result?
optionB: Passes: cut-out may be any value
optionC: Fails: cut-out is above the limit
optionD: Fails: cut-out is below the limit
explanation: Actual cut-out must never be above 1000 kPa (145 psi), so a cut-out of 1030 kPa fails. 1035 kPa is the safety valve figure, not a limit for cut-out.

question: In the governor test, the compressor does not cut back in until pressure falls to 540 kPa (78 psi). What is the result?
explanation: Actual cut-in must never be below 552 kPa (80 psi). A cut-in of 540 kPa fails the test.

question: For the air-loss rate test, how should the vehicle be set up?
optionA: Spring brakes off, engine off, pedal held
optionB: Spring brakes on, engine on, pedal free
optionC: Spring brakes off, engine on, pedal free
optionD: Spring brakes on, engine off, pedal held
explanation: Release the spring brakes, make sure pressure is in the normal range, shut off the engine and hold the brake pedal fully applied for one minute.

question: In the air-loss rate test, what about the pressure drop when the brakes are first applied?
explanation: Pressure drops noticeably when the brakes are first applied. That first drop is disregarded; the test starts once pressure has stabilized.

question: What is the maximum allowable air loss for a tractor with two or more trailers?
explanation: The handbook's limits are 21 kPa (3 psi) a minute for a straight truck, tractor or bus, 28 kPa (4 psi) for a tractor and trailer, and 41 kPa (6 psi) for a tractor with two or more trailers.

question: A tractor and one trailer lose 24 kPa in the minute after the first drop. What is the result, and why?
explanation: A tractor and trailer may lose up to 28 kPa (4 psi) a minute, so 24 kPa passes. The 21 kPa limit is for a straight truck, tractor or bus alone.

question: To test the tractor protection valve, you close the trailer supply valve and disconnect the service line coupler. What next?
optionA: Press and hold the brake pedal
optionC: Pull out the spring brake knob
explanation: With the supply valve closed and the service coupler placed where you can see it, press and hold the brake pedal and watch for air.

question: During the tractor protection valve test, air blows out of the disconnected service line coupler. What does this mean?
explanation: No air should exhaust from the trailer service line. If it does, the tractor protection valve is defective.

question: Which method does the handbook recommend for testing the automatic application of the trailer spring brakes?
optionC: Pulling out the trailer supply valve
explanation: Closing (pulling out) the supply valve is the recommended method. Disconnecting the supply line also works but is not recommended while it is under pressure.

question: How can you confirm that the trailer spring brakes have applied?
optionC: Push the supply valve back in
explanation: If you are not sure, gently add engine power to try to move forward or backward and confirm the brakes hold.

question: On a tractor and trailer, whose spring brakes is it preferable to use for the spring brake holding test?
explanation: The handbook says it is preferable to test the towing vehicle's spring brakes, where the trailer can be supplied air while the towing vehicle's parking brakes are released.

question: When draining the supply tank, how long should you let it drain?
optionB: Until only clean air comes out
explanation: Drain the supply tank until the valve discharges only clean air, then drain the remaining tanks.

question: You drain a secondary tank and visible oil comes out. What should you do?
explanation: Oil in any tank other than the supply tank risks contaminating the system, and the condition must be reported.

question: A significant amount of moisture drains from the supply tank, even though you drain it regularly. This may be:
explanation: The handbook says a significant quantity of moisture from the supply tank may be normal. The same amount from the other tanks is not normal and should be reported.

question: How often must brake adjustment (pushrod stroke) be inspected?
explanation: Brake wear varies, so the handbook says pushrod stroke must be inspected at least daily, and the Act requires a daily check.

question: What is the most common brake chamber size?
explanation: The handbook says the most common brake chamber size is 30, though sizes such as 16, 20, 24 and 36 are also used.

question: Without the owner's manual, how can you find a brake chamber's size?
explanation: Size is found by measuring the diameter of the clamp, which needs a special tool, or by finding the size markings on the chamber.

question: Where are you most likely to learn the brake chamber sizes on a vehicle?
explanation: The handbook says you are most likely to learn chamber sizes from your employer or the owner's manual, which avoids measuring.

question: What is the most visible and permanent sign of a long-stroke brake chamber?
explanation: Long-stroke chambers have square ports, a trapezoidal tag and body markings. The square ports are the most visible and permanent sign. Standard chambers have round ports.

question: On a long-stroke chamber, what does the trapezoidal tag under the clamp bolt show?
explanation: The tag shows the chamber's maximum stroke dimension. The handbook stresses that this is not the brake adjustment limit.

question: The adjustment limits of standard and long-stroke chambers can differ by how much?
explanation: Chamber type affects the limit, which can vary by 19 millimetres or more between standard and long-stroke chambers.

question: Using the two-measurement method, the pushrod reads 40 mm released and 85 mm applied. What is the applied stroke?
explanation: Subtract measurement 1 (released) from measurement 2 (applied): 85 - 40 = 45 mm.

question: To check brake adjustment, the primary and secondary gauges should read:
explanation: Raise or lower pressure until both gauges show 621 to 690 kPa (90 to 100 psi), then shut off the engine and fully apply the service brakes.

question: Brake adjustment is checked with the service brakes fully applied and the spring brakes:
explanation: The handbook says adjustment is inspected with the engine off, service brakes fully applied and spring brakes released.

question: What is the adjustment limit for a standard type 30 clamp-type chamber?
explanation: The handbook's chart gives 2 in (51 mm) for a standard type 30 chamber.

question: What is the adjustment limit for a type 30 LS chamber (long stroke with square ports)?
explanation: The chart gives 2-1/2 in (64 mm) for a type 30 LS chamber, longer than the 2 in (51 mm) of a standard type 30.

question: What is the adjustment limit for a standard type 24 clamp-type chamber?
explanation: The chart gives 1-3/4 in (45 mm) for a standard type 24 chamber.

question: A standard type 30 chamber shows an applied stroke of 55 mm. What is its condition?
optionC: Within its limit only on a trailer
explanation: The limit for a standard type 30 is 51 mm (2 in). 55 mm exceeds it, so the brake is out of adjustment and the vehicle is defective.

question: A type 30 LS chamber shows an applied stroke of 55 mm. What is its condition?
optionB: Out of adjustment on a bus
explanation: A type 30 LS chamber's limit is 64 mm (2-1/2 in), so 55 mm is within it.

question: What is the adjustment limit for a type 30 DD3 chamber on a bus or coach?
explanation: The chart lists the type 30 DD3 (bus/coach) chamber at 2-1/4 in (57 mm).

question: In Ontario, a driver may re-adjust manual slack adjusters only if the driver:
optionC: Finds the brake near its limit
explanation: Drivers who have a valid Ontario air brake adjustment certificate may re-adjust brakes with manual slack adjusters. A Z endorsement alone does not allow it.

question: A driver certified to re-adjust manual slack adjusters finds an automatic slack adjuster out of adjustment. Who may re-adjust it?
optionC: Any driver with a Z endorsement
explanation: The driver certification does not cover automatic slack adjusters. Only certified technicians may re-adjust or repair them.

question: An automatic slack adjuster keeps needing re-adjustment. What does this mean?
explanation: Working automatic slack adjusters do not need regular re-adjustment. If periodic re-adjustment is needed, the adjuster is defective and must be repaired by a certified technician.

question: Does brake adjustment still need to be inspected on brakes with automatic slack adjusters?
explanation: The handbook says inspection of brake adjustment must be carried out whether automatic or manual slack adjusters are used.
